findings.message: This only fixes the named cases. leaks() checks strings, Secret instances, own enumerable keys and values, Map, Set and typed arrays. Everything else passes as clean: functions and closures (`typeof value !== "object"` returns false), non-enumerable properties (Error.message and Error.cause), private `#fields`, getters on the prototype, a bare ArrayBuffer (not a view, so it has no enumerable keys), and Promises. Fix: reject any function result. Walk Error message, cause and name. Treat ArrayBuffer like a view. Refuse class instances that are not plain objects, arrays, Map, Set or Date unless they are known to be safe. Add these to the AC-2 variant table.
findings.scenario: useSecret(job, {connector:'xero',purpose:'x'}, async () => new Error(VALUE)) returns an Error whose message is the plaintext, and no SecretLeakError is thrown. useSecret(..., async (s) => () => s.reveal()) returns a closure that the caller can invoke later, outside the audited use. new TextEncoder().encode(VALUE).buffer passes too.

findings.message: Two gaps in decoding encoded runs. (1) decodedHolds checks the decoded text only against the raw values, not formsOf(value). Base64 of a JSON or form body that holds the value escaped is therefore missed. (2) Each run is decoded only from its first character. ENCODED_RUN also matches '/', '_', '-' and '+', so a run that starts with a prefix whose length is not a multiple of 4 (a URL path, for example) decodes misaligned, and the value is never found. Fix: compare the decoded text against formsOf(values), and decode each run at all four start offsets (and its base64url twin). Add both cases to the AC-2 table.
findings.scenario: With the test's VALUE, which contains a quote: returning Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({client_secret: VALUE})).toString('base64') decodes to text holding `q\"uo`, not the raw VALUE, so the result is accepted. Throwing new Error('GET https://idp.example/v1/' + base64('client-id:' + VALUE)) leaves the run 'example/v1/…' 11 characters misaligned, so it is not scrubbed.

findings.message: This is an instance fix for the missing use permission. The finding asked for authorization scoped per connector and per caller kind. recordUse authorizes the single action 'secrets:credential:use', and the connector is not part of what the authorizer sees: the test's authorizer is (ctx, action). So any actor allowed to use one connector can decrypt every connector, including msgraph-write. Fix: authorize per connector (for example `secrets:credential:use:${connector}`, or pass the connector as the resource), and cover xero vs msgraph-write and ui vs job callers in a table-driven test.
findings.scenario: The xero-sync job context (or any role granted secrets:credential:use for Xero) calls useSecret(ctx, {connector:'msgraph-write', purpose:'x'}, …). The call is authorized and the msgraph-write plaintext is returned.

findings.message: The fix for the blocker (data key cached before commit) is proven by only one failure point: the version insert trigger. B2 requires a table over the variants, and the finding named the failure points: the version insert, the audit write, the event emit and the idempotency settle. Each of these can roll back after dataKeyFor. Make the test table-driven over those failure points. Also, the test creates trigger fail_github and never drops it, and setAuthorizer(() => true) is not reset in a finally block, so a failing assertion leaks state into later tests.
findings.scenario: Change the fix so it only skips the cache when the version insert fails. This test stays green, but a rollback at the audit or emit step would still lose credentials.

findings.message: The 'uncommitted' test compares the row's xmin with pg_current_xact_id_if_assigned(), which is the top-level transaction id. When the data_key insert runs inside a subtransaction (a SAVEPOINT, such as a nested drizzle tx.transaction or a service called inside another service's run), xmin is the subtransaction's xid, not the top-level one. The row then reads as committed and the key is cached before commit, which brings back the credential-loss path. The test covers only a top-level putSecret. Fix: do not infer commit state from xid. Create the data key in its own transaction on a separate connection, commit it, then re-read and cache it. Add a test that runs putSecret under a savepoint that rolls back.
findings.scenario: putSecret runs inside a savepoint on a tenant with no key. dataKeyFor inserts the row, xmin is the subxid, and uncommitted=false, so the key is cached. The outer transaction rolls back, but the next putSecret seals with the cached key and commits. After the cache expires a new key is wrapped and the committed ciphertexts can no longer be opened.

findings.message: The use is now audited and last_used_* updated in a transaction that commits before decryption runs in a second transaction. If decrypt fails (KMS error, a version revoked in between, or open() failing), the audit trail and the Keys screen still show a successful use with that purpose. Record the failure, or only report a use as done once decryption succeeded.
findings.scenario: KMS unwrap returns 503. useSecret throws, but the credential row shows 'last used just now, sync'.

findings.message: The sweep writes one aggregate audit row with no resourceId, so a per-credential audit lookup will not show that its version was revoked and its ciphertext destroyed. Consider one audited record per revoked credential, or set resourceId on each.

The picked expiry date is read as the end of the day in UTC (T23:59:59Z), not in the tenant's or the user's time zone. Ahead of UTC (LK, AU) the credential keeps working into the next local day. Behind UTC it stops before the chosen local day ends. The KeyForm default uses the same UTC slice, so the screen agrees with the stored value but not with what the user meant.
findings.scenario: An AU admin picks 2026-10-20. The value is stored as 2026-10-20T23:59:59Z, which is 09:59 on 21 Oct in Sydney, so the credential still works on 21 Oct local time.
